documents.text:
196 FERC ¶ 61,095
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER ADDRESSING ARGUMENTS RAISED ON REHEARING

(Issued August 3, 2026)

On March 19, 2026, the Commission issued an order granting a complaint (Complaint) filed by Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC (NIPSCO)   pursuant to sections 202(c), 306, and 309 of the Federal Power Act (FPA) and Rule 206 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, proposing revisions to the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (Tariff) to add a provision (Proposed Tariff Provision) to allocate the costs of keeping Units 17 and 18 of the Schahfer generating plant (collectively, Schahfer Units) in operation, in response to the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) December 23, 2025 Emergency Order No. 202-25-12 (DOE Order), under FPA section 202(c) and section 301 of the DOE Organization Act.
The Commission granted the Complaint and found that the Proposed Tariff Provision was just and reasonable, subject to modification and to the outcome of the 
proceeding in Docket No. ER25-3425.  On April 20, 2026, rehearing requests were   filed by:  (1) the Michigan Attorney General; (2) the Office of the Illinois Attorney General (Illinois Attorney General); and (3) certain Public Interest Organizations (PIO).
Pursuant to Allegheny Defense Project v. FERC, the rehearing requests filed in this proceeding may be deemed denied by operation of law.  However, as permitted by section 313(a) of the FPA, we are modifying the discussion in the Complaint Order and continue to reach the same result in this proceeding, as discussed below.  
Background
Schahfer Units Retirement Plan
The Schahfer Units, located in northwestern Indiana, are coal-fired units that   each has a maximum capacity of 437.5 MW.  NIPSCO planned to retire the units on December 31, 2025, pursuant to settlement agreements approved by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission in 2023 and 2025.  NIPSCO submitted a notice to suspend operation of the Schahfer Units to MISO pursuant to Attachment Y of the Tariff, and MISO found no reliability violations.
DOE Order
In the DOE Order, the Secretary of Energy determined that “an emergency exists in portions of the Midwest region of the United States due to a shortage of electric energy, a shortage of facilities for the generation of electric energy, and other causes.”  Further, the Secretary of Energy determined that issuance of the DOE Order will “meet the emergency and serve the public interest.”  Therefore, the Secretary of Energy directed MISO and NIPSCO to take all measures necessary to ensure that the Schahfer Units were available to operate and directed NIPSCO to keep the Schahfer Units open for 90 days, i.e., until March 23, 2026.  
The DOE Order cited a statement in the 2024 North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Long-Term Reliability Assessment that MISO is at risk because “probabilistic assessments indicate above-normal generator outages during extreme weather can result in unserved energy or load loss.  With uncertainty around new resource additions and existing generator retirements, MISO is also at risk of falling below [Reference Margin Levels] within the next five years.”  The DOE Order quoted a MISO April 2025 presentation on the Planning Resource Auction Results for Planning Year 2025-2026 (PRA) as demonstrating that, for the MISO North and MISO Central regions, which include Indiana, “new capacity additions were insufficient to offset the negative impacts of decreased accreditation, suspension/retirements and external resources[.]”  The DOE Order also referenced an annual survey conducted by the Organization of MISO States, Inc. (OMS) and MISO projecting that additional capacity is needed beyond current commitments to meet the projected summer 2026 Planning Reserve Margin and projecting that there would be shortfalls in capacity to meet the peak demand for electricity in each of the following four summers and winters.  The DOE Order noted that the OMS-MISO survey attributed these projected deficits to large quantities of existing generation capacity retirements and projected accelerated growth  of electric demand that would outpace the increase in generation capacity.  The DOE Order noted that MISO’s efforts to address its projected deficiencies to date, particularly through its Expedited Resource Addition Study (ERAS) process, would not immediately add new capacity due to commercial operation dates for ERAS resources that were at least three years away and supply chain constraints that would impede the construction of new capacity.  
The DOE Order directed NIPSCO to “file with [this Commission] Tariff revisions or waivers [necessary] to effectuate [the DOE Order].”
Several entities filed requests for rehearing of the DOE Order with DOE.  On  June 1, 2026, the DOE issued an order addressing arguments raised on rehearing, sustaining the result of the DOE Order.  
NIPSCO’s Complaint and Responsive Pleadings  
NIPSCO stated in the Complaint that it and MISO agreed that the Tariff does not have a mechanism for NIPSCO to recover costs incurred under the DOE Order.  NIPSCO therefore asked the Commission to exercise its authority under FPA sections 202(c), 306, and 309 to order MISO to adopt the Proposed Tariff Provision as a cost recovery and allocation mechanism.  NIPSCO also stated that the Proposed Tariff Provision was strictly to establish a cost allocation mechanism, and that, after the 90-day period, NIPSCO would submit a filing in a separate docket with the actual costs to be allocated according to the Tariff mechanism.  Specifically, NIPSCO stated that it would submit a subsequent filing to the Commission under section 202(c) in which NIPSCO would explain and support its just and reasonable costs associated with operating the Schahfer Units and complying with the DOE Order, net of market revenues.  
NIPSCO asserted that the Proposed Tariff Provision met the “just and reasonable” standard of section 202(c)(1).  In support, NIPSCO stated that section 202(c) requires costs to be allocated based on the scope and nature of the emergency and that the DOE Order referred to the MISO North and MISO Central regions; accordingly, NIPSCO argued that allocating NIPSCO’s costs of complying with the DOE Order to both the MISO North and MISO Central regions comports with section 202(c)’s just and reasonable standard.  NIPSCO noted that the Proposed Tariff Provision was similar to the Tariff provision approved by the Commission with regard to the Consumers Energy Company (Consumers) J.H. Campbell plant (Campbell Plant), and the geographic scope identified in the DOE Order was virtually identical to the scope identified in the DOE emergency order on the Campbell Plant (Campbell Plant DOE Order). 
The Proposed Tariff Provision specified that it was pursuant to the DOE Order  and applies to the allocation of costs (DOE Order Costs) associated with the continued availability of the Schahfer Units pursuant to the DOE Order and any extensions ordered by the Secretary of Energy.  The Proposed Tariff Provision stated that NIPSCO would petition the Commission to approve recovery of DOE Order Costs, net of market revenues, and that the costs would be allocated among Local Resource Zones 1-7, i.e., among zones in the MISO North and MISO Central regions, to load-serving entities (LSE) on a “load ratio share” basis.  NIPSCO noted that the issue of cost allocation       on a demand or energy basis is currently pending before the Commission in Docket No. ER25-3425 and that NIPSCO intended to defer to the Commission’s final decision   in that proceeding.
NIPSCO argued that the Commission’s prior notice requirements, filed rate doctrine, and rule against retroactive ratemaking apply to filings or proceedings under sections 205 and 206 of the FPA, but do not apply to determinations and cost recovery under section 202(c).  NIPSCO argued that section 202(c) allows costs to be determined and recovered after the emergency generation or provision of jurisdictional service.  NIPSCO maintained that section 202(c)’s contemplation of such post-hoc determinations and recovery is demonstrated in the wording of the statute, including that, after an emergency order “takes effect,” there will be “supplemental” orders regarding “compensation or reimbursement.” 
MISO agreed with NIPSCO that the existing Tariff did not contain a mechanism for cost allocation under these circumstances.  MISO stated that it did not oppose the Proposed Tariff Provision and that it would file such a schedule if directed by the Commission.  MISO noted that it reserved the right to change the cost allocation mechanism “to account for existing Tariff requirements and to include other clarifications as may be appropriate.”  
Complaint Order
The Commission granted NIPSCO’s Complaint and found that the Proposed Tariff Provision was just and reasonable under FPA section 202(c).
The Commission noted that the DOE Organization Act gives the Secretary of Energy the authority pursuant to FPA section 202(c) to take action to address an energy emergency.  The Commission further indicated that section 202(c)(1) also provides for affected parties to agree on terms or have them proscribed.
Applying the cost causation principle, the Commission found that it was just and reasonable to allocate costs in accordance with the scope of the emergency as described by the DOE Order.  The Commission acknowledged that parties presented different interpretations of how the DOE Order defined the geographic scope of the emergency.  Consistent with NIPSCO’s interpretation, the Commission found that the most reasonable reading of the DOE Order’s intended scope was that the emergency necessitating the continued operation of the Schahfer Units was in the MISO North and MISO Central regions, i.e., Local Resource Zones 1-7.  The Commission found that allocating the DOE Order Costs using a load-ratio-share method based on peak demand is justified, citing the Commission’s reasoning that a load-ratio-share allocation method based on actual peak demand reasonably aligned the allocation of the Campbell Plant DOE Order costs with the emergency and the beneficiaries of the Campbell Plant’s continued operation.  The Commission also found that a separate stakeholder process was unnecessary and that any interested stakeholder had an opportunity to comment in the NIPSCO Complaint proceeding. 
The Commission rejected certain arguments against adoption of the Proposed Tariff Provision, finding they were beyond the limited scope of the proceeding.  Such arguments included issues related to the prudence of costs associated with operating the Schahfer Units and whether the DOE Order authorizes repairs to the Schahfer Units, particularly Schahfer Unit 18.  The Commission also rejected as beyond the scope of the proceeding the question of whether the provision should include a mechanism to refund upgrade costs recovered under the Proposed Tariff Provision should the Schahfer Units continue to operate beyond the term of the DOE Order.  Additionally, the Commission disagreed with Public Interest Organizations that NIPSCO must demonstrate what, if any, uncompensated benefits are provided by the continued operation of the Schahfer Units and that the recovery of DOE Order Costs is covered by existing Tariff provisions, particularly the Tariff’s Value of Lost Load (VOLL) mechanism.  The Commission found that existing Tariff provisions did not provide a cost allocation method for prudently incurred costs associated with orders issued under FPA section 202(c) directing resources to ensure continuing availability for operation, such as the DOE Order Costs.  The Commission further found that, under the Proposed Tariff Provision, any market revenue, including any revenue based on scarcity pricing, would be netted from the DOE Order Costs, and that recovery of any DOE Order Costs in excess of market revenue was outside the scope of the Complaint proceeding.  The Commission noted that parties could raise issues related to the scope of costs prudently incurred pursuant to the DOE Order, including costs for repairs to the Schahfer Units, in a separate proceeding when NIPSCO seeks approval to recover specific DOE Order Costs.
Furthermore, the Commission rejected arguments that it could not approve compensation that arose from the Schahfer Units’ capacity benefits.  The Commission found that, regardless of whether the Schahfer Units are treated as capacity resources in MISO’s resource adequacy construct, the DOE Order cited resource adequacy concerns for the MISO North and MISO Central regions as the driver of the need for continued operation of the Schahfer Units.
Requests for Rehearing
Rehearing petitioners argue that the Commission erred in:  (1) failing to order a stakeholder process before issuing the Complaint Order; (2) failing to order a hearing before issuing the Complaint Order; (3) mis-applying cost causation principles; (4) incorrectly defining the scope of the emergency; and (5) improperly relying on an unlawful emergency declaration.
Discussion
We sustain the result of the Complaint Order and continue to find the Proposed Tariff Provision just and reasonable under FPA section 202(c).  For the reasons discussed below, we are not persuaded by arguments on rehearing that this finding should be reversed.  
Need for Stakeholder Process 
Requests for Rehearing
The Illinois Attorney General contends that the Commission erred by declining to require MISO to initiate a stakeholder process to ensure that ratepayers have a forum to address cost allocation and to ensure that rates are just and reasonable.  The Illinois Attorney General argues that this is particularly important when there are ratepayers who are not benefiting from, nor causing, the costs.  The Illinois Attorney General notes that, unlike Indiana and many other MISO states, Illinois is not vertically integrated.  The Illinois Attorney General asserts that, in effect, the Proposed Tariff Provision shifts costs that are generally part of an integrated utility’s rates onto residents in other MISO states, without regard to the needs of each state. 
Commission Determination
We continue to find that a stakeholder process related to the Proposed Tariff Provision is not necessary.  The instant proceeding has provided any interested stakeholder notice of NIPSCO’s proposal and an opportunity to comment, including a further opportunity on rehearing.  The Commission has broad discretion to determine issues before it—including making a determination that no further process is necessary  to decide an issue.  Here, the Commission, in its discretion, found that further process was not necessary given that the record provided a sufficient basis for the Commission’s acceptance of NIPSCO’s proposal.  Similarly, we disagree with the Illinois Attorney General’s contention that a stakeholder process is required to develop more detailed assessments of the benefits for various MISO regions and customers, because there   was already sufficient evidence in the record for the Commission to reach such a determination.
Need for Evidentiary Hearing 
Requests for Rehearing
The Michigan Attorney General claims that the Commission was required to    hold a hearing under FPA section 202(c)(1) before granting the Complaint.  The Michigan Attorney General claims that the language in section 202(c)(1), which states that the Commission may issue a supplemental order “after hearing held either before     or after such order takes effect,” requires a hearing to be held before the Commission issues an order.  The Michigan Attorney General claims that Commission rules create procedures for hearings, and such procedures have not been noticed or held in this case.  The Michigan Attorney General alleges that this failure constitutes a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) given that holding a hearing is an “unambiguous” obligation under the FPA.  The Michigan Attorney General claims that it has been prejudiced by this failure by being denied the opportunity to present evidence and further develop the record during a hearing.
Commission Determination
The Commission met the hearing requirement under FPA section 202(c)(1) by considering the pleadings on the record in the initial order.  We are not persuaded that the Commission was required to hold a trial-type evidentiary hearing before granting the Complaint.  The “scope of the ‘opportunity for a hearing’ protected by the FPA”       does not extend to situations “‘where [the Commission] can decide as a matter of law’” or when a party fails “to point to specific disputed facts.”  “A trial-type evidentiary hearing is unnecessary when there are no material facts in dispute that cannot be resolved on the basis of the written record.  The Commission has discretion regarding the process for deciding the issues before it and does not need to hold a hearing where, as here, it   can resolve disputes on the basis of the record before it.”  Here, the Michigan Attorney General states that it was denied the opportunity to “further develop and present evidence,” but it does not explain why it could not have provided such evidence at an earlier stage of this proceeding (e.g., in its protest) or otherwise provide an indication of the nature of the evidence it would have put forward.  As explained in the Complaint Order, the Commission determined it already had a sufficient basis to accept NIPSCO’s proposal without further process.  We continue to find that there are no disputed issues of material fact relevant to the issue presented in this proceeding and thus that the Commission was not required to hold a trial-type evidentiary hearing in response to the Complaint.
Cost Causation
Requests for Rehearing
The Illinois Attorney General and PIOs argue that the Commission violated the requirement in FPA section 202(c) that rates be just and reasonable, which encompasses the cost causation principle that customers that pay for a facility must benefit from that facility’s operation.  
The Illinois Attorney General argues that the Complaint Order, like the DOE Order, is not supported by substantial evidence and fails to ensure that cost recovery and cost allocation are just and reasonable.  The Illinois Attorney General asserts that the Commission failed to identify any reliability benefit that may be realized by customers outside the NIPSCO territory associated with the Schahfer Units and did not address how NIPSCO’s status as a vertically integrated utility may affect cost allocation.  Specifically, the Illinois Attorney General maintains that the Commission should consider more than load ratio in MISO’s North and Central regions.  The Illinois Attorney General asserts that the Commission should also consider whether the Schahfer Units are being retained to serve large load and contends that customers who may benefit, including large load customers, should not be subsidized by the rest of MISO North and Central customers.  
PIOs argue that the Commission failed to address their argument that no costs should be recovered for Schahfer Unit 18 because that unit has been inoperable since before the issuance of the DOE Order and ratepayers should not have to pay to repair it.  PIOs note that they previously argued that (1) any costs incurred to repair Schahfer Unit 18 are imprudent because DOE does not have authority under section 202(c) to require NIPSCO to revive a non-operational generation facility, and (2) NIPSCO should not be able to seek cost recovery for Schahfer Unit 18 while it is not functional and unable to provide any benefits to the MISO region.  PIOs maintain that, while the Commission responded to the first argument, it failed to respond to the second.  PIOs argue that the Commission “may impose an exception to the used-and-useful standard to allow recovery of prudent costs for the non-used plant, but it must justify this decision.”  PIOs argue that the Commission must answer the threshold question of whether allowing such an exception reasonably balances consumers’ interests in fair rates against investors’ interests.
In addition, PIOs argue that the Commission has not explained why over-procurement of capacity provides a benefit to ratepayers or what benefits remain uncompensated under the current Tariff.  PIOs assert that the Commission did not address arguments that the Schahfer Units did not provide a capacity benefit because each zone in MISO had already met its capacity obligation.  PIOs maintain that the Complaint Order undermines previous Commission findings that over-procuring capacity can lead to unjust and unreasonable rates and that the MISO resource adequacy construct is just and reasonable.   
PIOs further argue that the Commission also failed to adequately respond to  PIOs’ argument that current Tariff provisions fully compensate the Schahfer Units for any cognizable benefits they may provide MISO customers.  PIOs argue that the Commission’s statement that the existing Tariff provisions “do not provide a cost allocation method for prudently incurred costs associated [with] orders issued under    FPA section 202(c)” is nonresponsive to PIOs’ argument that the allocated costs are      not associated with commensurate benefits.  PIOs assert that it remains unclear what uncompensated benefits the Schahfer Units are providing, given that the Schahfer Units are not providing capacity benefits and their real-time reliability contribution is already compensated through VOLL pricing.  
PIOs also argue that the Commission has not explained how demand-based       load ratio share properly allocates costs according to benefits.  PIOs maintain that the relative benefit each of MISO’s Local Resource Zones 1-7 will receive from the delayed retirement of the Schahfer Units remains unclear, as does the reasonableness of allocating costs using a demand-based load-ratio-share method.  PIOs note that, although the Commission stated that it found a load-ratio-share method based on peak demand to be justified in a parallel proceeding regarding cost allocation for the Campbell Plant, the Commission order did not explain why load ratio share properly allocated costs amongst the zones.  PIOs further argue that, unlike the Campbell Plant proceeding, where the relevant section 202(c) order was silent on whether the Campbell Plant could be considered a capacity resource, the DOE Order here prohibits considering the Schahfer Units as a capacity resource.  
PIOs argue that the record in this proceeding contains no evidence that benefits from the Schahfer Units will accrue roughly proportionate to zonal peak demand.  PIOs suggest that, even if Zones 1-7 were short on capacity, zones with larger quantities of excess capacity would presumably need less of the capacity from the Schahfer Units than zones with less excess capacity.  PIOs add that even if the Schahfer Units are needed to meet future demand, allocating costs using current zonal demand is unjustified because the future peak load contributions and available resource levels will dictate future capacity needs.
Lastly, PIOs assert that allocating all costs on a demand basis still may not be justified because it does not capture all of the Schahfer Units’ benefit streams.  PIOs argue that any revenue from the Schahfer Units’ participation in the energy and ancillary services markets untethers the ultimate cost of the units from any resource adequacy benefit they may be providing, making it even less tenable to allocate costs based on a demand, rather than energy, basis.  
Commission Determination
We remain unpersuaded by the Illinois Attorney General’s and PIOs’ arguments.
First, we find that the issue of whether additional capacity is needed remains outside the scope of this proceeding, which only concerns whether to grant NIPSCO’s complaint and direct MISO to adopt the Proposed Tariff Revision as the just and reasonable replacement rate.  Under the DOE Organization Act, the determination of the need for the operation of the Schahfer Units rests solely with DOE; the Commission’s responsibility is to provide for “compensation or reimbursement” of the costs of operation.  We therefore reject PIOs’ argument on this point.
We also disagree with PIOs that the Commission has failed to identify the  benefits the Schahfer Units provide, consider all of the units’ benefit streams, or otherwise justify how a demand-based load-ratio-share method properly allocates costs   in accordance with benefits.  We likewise disagree with the Illinois Attorney General that the Commission should consider more than load ratio or that the Commission failed to identify any reliability benefits.  As stated above, it is DOE’s role to determine whether an emergency exists and to exercise its judgment in prescribing actions that     will best address that emergency and serve the public interest.  To the extent that PIOs assert that the record lacks evidence that benefits from the Schahfer Units will accrue roughly proportionate to zonal peak demand, NIPSCO is not required to make further demonstrations of the beneficiaries of a DOE order pursuant to FPA section 202(c) when the DOE order identifies a resource adequacy emergency for the MISO North and MISO Central regions.  
Moreover, in the Campbell Plant proceeding, the Commission found that a load-ratio-share method based on the forecasted season coincident peak demand reasonably aligns the allocation of DOE Order Costs with the emergency described by DOE and    the beneficiaries of addressing that emergency.  On compliance in that proceeding,    the Commission further explained that the unrecovered fixed costs to operate and maintain the Campbell Plant “are primarily driven by peak period demands, such that      a demand-based allocation of the remaining net costs of the continued operation of the Campbell Plant pursuant to the [Campbell Plant DOE orders] aligns with cost causation principles.”  Contrary to PIOs’ suggestion otherwise, the DOE orders in that proceeding were not silent regarding whether the relevant units could be considered a capacity resource, and neither those orders nor the DOE Order here prohibits the Commission from approving compensation arising from the relevant units’ capacity benefits.  Accordingly, we continue to find the Campbell Plant reasoning applicable here.  
We summarily dismiss the Illinois Attorney General’s and PIOs’ remaining arguments that the Complaint Order violated cost causation principles.  These arguments were addressed in the Complaint Order.  Specifically, PIOs again argue:  (1) that the Commission has not explained why over-procurement of capacity provides a benefit to ratepayers or what benefits remain uncompensated under the current tariff; and (2) that the Commission erred by failing to respond to questions as to whether the Schahfer Units could be treated as capacity resources.  The Commission addressed these arguments in the Complaint Order, and we remain unpersuaded by these arguments for the same reasons as stated in the Complaint Order, wherein the Commission found that it was just and reasonable for the cost allocation method to allocate costs in accordance with the scope of the emergency as described by the DOE Order and that the most reasonable reading of the DOE Order’s intended scope is that the emergency necessitating the continued operation of the Schahfer Units is in Local Resource Zones 1-7.  Regardless of whether the Schahfer Units are treated as capacity resources in MISO’s resource adequacy construct, the DOE Order cited resource adequacy concerns for the MISO North and MISO Central regions as the driver of the need for continued operation of the Schahfer Units.  We continue to find that the existing Tariff provisions (e.g., VOLL pricing) did not provide a cost allocation method for prudently incurred costs associated with orders issued under FPA section 202(c) directing resources to ensure continuing availability for operation, such as the DOE Order Costs.  We also reiterate our finding that parties may raise issues related to the scope of costs prudently incurred pursuant to the DOE Order, including costs for repairs to the Schahfer Units, in the separate cost recovery proceeding.  Similarly, as to PIOs’ argument that the Commission failed to consider that Schahfer Unit 18 is non-operational and cannot provide any benefits to MISO customers, we find that such arguments may be raised in the separate cost recovery proceeding.  The DOE Orders determined that Schahfer Unit 18 provides benefits to MISO customers, such that challenging that finding is beyond the scope of this proceeding.  Moreover, issues regarding which specific costs were incurred in meeting the requirements of the DOE Orders are more appropriately raised in the separate cost recovery proceeding.
Lastly, the Illinois Attorney General raises for the first time on rehearing arguments regarding whether the Schahfer Units are being retained to serve large load and that the Commission needed to address how NIPSCO’s status as a vertically integrated utility may affect cost allocation.  PIOs also raise for the first time on rehearing that the Commission failed to consider the “used and useful” standard with respect to Schahfer Unit 18.  Under longstanding precedent, we do not consider arguments or new evidence raised for the first time on rehearing, subject to a narrow exception for matters that could not have been previously presented, e.g., claims based on information that only recently became available or concerns prompted by a change in material circumstances.  We have adopted this approach “because (1) our regulations preclude other parties from responding to a request for rehearing, and (2) such behavior is disruptive to the administrative process because it has the effect of moving the target for 
parties seeking a final administrative decision.”  The Illinois Attorney General and PIOs had the opportunity to raise these arguments before the Complaint Order, but did not do so.  Accordingly, these arguments are procedurally barred.  Moreover, even       if these arguments were properly before us, we continue to find that it is just and reasonable for the cost allocation method to allocate costs in accordance with the scope   of the emergency as described by the DOE Order.     
Scope of Emergency
Requests for Rehearing
The Michigan Attorney General contends that the Commission in the Complaint Order was arbitrary and capricious in finding that “the most reasonable reading” of the DOE Order’s intended scope is that the emergency necessitating the continued operation 
of the Schahfer Units is in the MISO North and MISO Central regions.  The    Michigan Attorney General claims that the evidence for this finding is limited to              a sentence from the DOE Order quoting MISO’s PRA, stating that “new capacity additions were insufficient to offset the negative impacts of decreased accreditation, suspension/retirements and external resources.”  The Michigan Attorney General argues that the DOE Order itself does not limit the emergency to particular zones in MISO, but rather addresses a MISO-wide emergency.  PIOs state that the DOE Order improperly disregarded the resource adequacy efforts and findings of state authorities, MISO, and the Commission, which have already ensured that the MISO North and MISO Central zones have “sufficient capacity.”  
The Michigan Attorney General claims that the Commission deviated from precedent when it determined that the scope of the benefit of the implementation of the DOE Order was best determined by considering the scope of the emergency described in the DOE Order.  The Michigan Attorney General posits that, “[a]ssuming arguendo the validity of the DOE Order,” the benefits of operating the Schahfer Units to comply with a federal law would accrue throughout the region.  The Michigan Attorney General states, as an example, that, where New York State law required investment in infrastructure for state goals, the Commission used cost causation principles to allocate the costs across New York State.  The Michigan Attorney General suggests that no objective benefit exists for Local Resource Zones 1-7 from the continued operation of the Schahfer Units given that NIPSCO and MISO had already accounted for the retirement of the Schahfer Units in capacity planning through Integrated Resource Plan and Attachment Y processes.  The Michigan Attorney General suggests that the Commission’s reliance on the DOE Order is therefore misplaced given that the DOE Order, in turn, cites to parts of a MISO presentation that were discussing the whole PRA rather than only the MISO North and MISO Central zones.  Thus, the Michigan Attorney General accuses the Commission of relying on the DOE Order’s false characterization of the PRA results as pertaining to Local Resource Zones 1-7.  
Commission Determination
We are unpersuaded by the Michigan Attorney General’s and PIOs’ arguments.
First, as discussed above, the issue of whether additional capacity is needed remains outside the scope of the Complaint Order, which only addressed whether to grant NIPSCO’s complaint and direct MISO to adopt the Proposed Tariff Revision as the just and reasonable replacement rate.  The determination of the need for the operation of the Schahfer Units rests solely with DOE; the Commission’s responsibility is to provide for “compensation or reimbursement” of the costs of operation.  We therefore reject the Michigan Attorney General’s and PIOs’ arguments on this point.
We are not persuaded by arguments that the Complaint Order’s finding that it was just and reasonable to allocate costs associated with the continued availability of the Schahfer Units to MISO’s Local Resource Zones 1-7, in accordance with the scope of the emergency as described by the DOE Order, was insufficiently supported by the record.  The Michigan Attorney General’s and PIOs’ arguments do not refute the fact that the DOE Order references Local Resource Zones 1-7 as the location of the emergency.  While we acknowledge that the DOE Order references energy shortfalls and other concerns beyond MISO’s Local Resource Zones 1-7, we continue to find that the        most reasonable reading of the DOE Order’s intended scope is that the emergency necessitating the continued operation of the Schahfer Units is in Local Resource       Zones 1-7 for the reasons stated in the Complaint Order.  
We also disagree with the Michigan Attorney General’s argument that the Commission was inconsistent in the Complaint Order with its precedent in Niagara Mohawk.  In that case, New York State law required investment in transmission infrastructure for state goals, and the Commission found that the utility’s proposal to allocate the costs of that transmission infrastructure statewide was consistent with cost causation principles.  As an initial matter, Niagara Mohawk did not arise in the FPA section 202(c) context or address the appropriate definition of a geographic scope of a declared emergency.  Regardless, we do not see the reasoning of Niagara Mohawk as inconsistent with the Commission’s reasoning in this proceeding.  In Niagara Mohawk, the Commission found persuasive evidence showing that the transmission project at issue would have statewide benefits, and thus the Commission found it just and reasonable to allocate the costs of the project statewide.  Here, the Commission in the Complaint Order found that the intended beneficiaries of the DOE Order were the LSEs in Local Resource Zones 1-7 and approved the allocation of the costs to those LSEs.
Reliance on Emergency Declaration
Requests for Rehearing
The Michigan Attorney General and PIOs maintain that the Complaint Order relies on an unlawful emergency declaration.  The Michigan Attorney General asserts that the DOE Order is currently being challenged in separate proceedings, and the Commission is not authorized to grant a cost recovery mechanism absent statutory authorization.  The Michigan Attorney General claims that the Commission could have deferred action on setting a cost recovery mechanism and failed to engage meaningfully with arguments in favor of deferral.  The Michigan Attorney General argues that FPA section 202(c) gives the Commission discretion to resolve cost recovery questions and contains no temporal requirement.  The Michigan Attorney General also argues that there is no benefit to initiating a cost recovery mechanism now, and significant harm could result from prematurely initiating a cost recovery mechanism.  The Michigan Attorney General contends that, if the DOE Order is ultimately found invalid, then cost recovery under the Complaint Order would become unjust and unreasonable and constitute a filed-rate doctrine violation.  The Michigan Attorney General states        that the Commission would need to refund charges to MISO’s customers because the Commission “has no power to alter a rate retroactively.”  As a result, the Michigan Attorney General argues, significant risk exists to MISO customers if improper costs    are collected, along with a risk of avoidable administrative costs that will be required to attempt to unwind that cost recovery.  The Michigan Attorney General claims that     the Commission provided no explanation for rejecting its arguments in favor of a stay, despite the Commission being obligated to give a reason for its rejection.  Lastly, the Michigan Attorney General argues that the Commission failed to explain why its refusal to defer a decision would better serve “to mitigate potential regulatory uncertainty,” particularly in light of the additional litigation on the Commission’s decision to grant Consumers’ complaint.
Commission Determination
As discussed above, the issues raised regarding the validity of the DOE Order are outside the scope of the Complaint Order, which only addressed whether to grant NIPSCO’s complaint and direct MISO to adopt the Proposed Tariff Revision as the just and reasonable replacement rate.  The Commission’s responsibility is to provide for “compensation or reimbursement” of the costs of operation pursuant to an FPA section 202(c) order issued    by DOE.  While the Michigan Attorney General suggests that there is no “order to be implemented” because it has challenged the validity of the DOE Order in a pending proceeding before the D.C. Circuit, the DOE Order has not been stayed or invalidated.  We therefore reject the Michigan Attorney General’s and PIOs’ claims that the Complaint Order relies on an unlawful emergency declaration.
We sustain the Commission’s decision in the Complaint Order rejecting requests to delay action on the Proposed Tariff Provision pending further litigation of the DOE Order.  The Commission acted well within its discretion by promptly acting on NIPSCO’s complaint, thereby helping to mitigate potential regulatory uncertainty.
We also deny the Michigan Attorney General’s request for stay and disagree     with its assertion that the Commission failed to assess how deferral would avoid inefficiencies.  First, the Michigan Attorney General’s request has not satisfied          the Commission’s filing requirements to request a motion for stay.  But, even if the request was not deficient, we nevertheless would find it unpersuasive on the merits.      The Commission reviews requests for stay under the standard established by the APA:     a stay will be granted if the Commission finds that “justice so requires.”  Under this standard, the Commission considers such factors as:  (1) whether the moving party will suffer irreparable injury without a stay, (2) whether a stay would substantially harm other parties, and (3) whether the stay is in the public interest.  The Commission’s general policy is to refrain from granting stays in order to assure definiteness and finality in its proceedings.  If the party requesting the stay is unable to demonstrate that it will suffer 

irreparable harm absent a stay, we need not examine the other factors.  As the D.C. Circuit has explained, the standard for showing irreparable harm is strict:  
[T]he injury must be both certain and great; it must be actual and not theoretical. . . . It is also well settled that economic loss does not, in and of itself, constitute irreparable harm. . . . Mere injuries, however substantial, in terms of money, time and energy necessarily expended in the absence of a stay are not enough.  The possibility that adequate compensatory or other corrective relief will be available at a later date, in the ordinary course of litigation weighs heavily against a claim of irreparable harm.
The Michigan Attorney General has not demonstrated that any financial harm MISO ratepayers may face is irreparable and could not otherwise be relieved in the ordinary course of litigation, including through refunds, if warranted.  Nor has it made any showing that a stay would be in the public interest.  A desire to avoid potential economic and administrative costs is insufficient to warrant a stay.  Accordingly,      we deny the Michigan Attorney General’s request for stay of the Complaint Order.
The Commission orders:

In response to the requests for rehearing, the Complaint Order is hereby modified and the result sustained, as discussed in the body of this order.

By the Commission.
